paragraphs: While all creations display some degree of order and intelligence, the human soul is marked by a deeper hunger: to seek meaning, purpose, relationship, values, moral truth, and freedom. These are not incidental traits but emanations of the creator itself, echoes of its own nature imprinted on the human soul. It is humanity’s nature, then, to seek meaning where alone it can be found: in the creator itself, by extending its presence throughout creation.

Because the creator is nurturing, benevolent, good, and constructive, humanity’s highest calling is to imitate these very qualities. This principle of imitatio Dei becomes the deepest foundation for values, morality, and virtue— not invented by humanity, but received as an extension of the creator’s own nature. It is through these same values that the creator’s presence is extended through humanity: wherever a people aligns its purpose and values with the creator’s own, it does not merely survive but flourishes and lasts; wherever it turns away, it withers [25]—a truth Mozi echoes from the East: those who follow Heaven’s will and love universally are blessed; those who defy it meet calamity [26]. This pattern, arguably more than any other, has shaped the long arc of human history.

This conviction echoes across traditions. Augustine and Pascal both locate an unquenchable hunger in the human heart that only the creator can satisfy [27, 28]. Scripture calls humanity to imitate this nature directly, urging believers to “be imitators of God” [29]. From the East, Laozi teaches that Dao De— literally the creator’s own nurturing virtue and emanation—names the very moral principle humanity is called to embody [30]. Even modern psychology concurs: Frankl locates humanity’s deepest drive in selftranscendence, an echo of the self-giving nature humanity is called to imitate [38]. Together, these voices affirm one truth: humanity’s deepest hunger is answered only by the creator, and only as it embraces the creator’s likeness does human life flourish.
